deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. The page is a numerical check of a two-lens telescope objective. Both lenses are menisci convex toward the object: a crown positive meniscus and a flint negative meniscus. This is the design type Gauss published in 1817 (the 'Gauss objective'). The page computes the back focal distance for three colours in two ways: by paraxial (first-order) formulas and by an exact trigonometric trace of a marginal ray. The difference is the longitudinal spherical aberration of each colour. The computation is done once with the flint radii r''=42.06817, r'''=28.07073, and again with the corrected flint radii r''=42.07205 ('Neuer Werth von r''', log = 1.6239937) and r'''=28.07232. All numbers are 7-place logarithms; a characteristic 9 or 8 means -1 or -2 (e.g. 9.5014764 = log sin 18 deg 30').

DATA (decoded).
- Crown: r = 34.15287 (log 1.5334273), r' = 101.33007 (log 2.0057383), thickness 2.
- The header (n-1)/r = 0.015084 and (n-1)/r' = 0.005084 give n-1 = 0.51516 for the middle colour. So the crown radii are scaled so that the crown alone has power (n-1)(1/r - 1/r') = 0.01, i.e. f = 100.
- Crown indices (log n): 0.1773483, 0.1804591, 0.1835477, i.e. n = 1.50435, 1.51516, 1.52608 (three colours, say red/mean/violet).
- Air gap 0.5.
- Flint: R3 = 42.06817 (-log = 8.3760463), R4 = 28.07073 (-log = 8.5517463), thickness 0.8.
- Flint indices (log n): 0.1991543, 0.2046002, 0.2099785, i.e. n = 1.58182, 1.60177, 1.62167.
- All four centres of curvature lie on the image side.

A. PARAXIAL TRACE (top block), done in the 'reduced' form 1/((n-1)s). The same steps are done for each colour.
1. Crown first surface. log[n/(n-1)] = 0.4746180, 0.4685153, 0.4625818, so s1' = n r/(n-1) = 101.86977, 100.44830, 99.08527. Subtracting the thickness gives 99.86977, 98.44830, 97.08527 (logs 1.9994340, ...).
2. Crown second surface. -log(n-1) = 0.2972697, ... From 1/s2' = n/s2 - (n-1)/r' one gets s2' = 99.14918, 97.02673, 94.99224, written as log[1/((n-1)s2')] = 8.3009808, 8.3011648, 8.3013460.
   - Check (my identification): 10^(8.3009808-10) + 1/r' = 0.0199977 + 0.009868739 = 0.029866478 = n/((n-1)s2). The values 0.029874945 and 0.029883297 are the same check for the other colours; 0.009868739 = 1/r'.
3. Air gap. Subtract 0.5: 98.64918, 96.52673, 94.49224.
4. Flint first surface. -log(n_f-1) = 0.2352188, 0.2205695, 0.2063982.
   - 1/((n_f-1)s3) = 0.017423096, 0.017215589, 0.017021667.
   - Add 1/R3 = 0.023770940 (new value 1/42.07205 = 0.023768749). The sum is n_f/((n_f-1)s3'), with log 8.6148344, 8.6126411, 8.6105814.
   - Hence s3' = 66.0, and subtracting the flint thickness, log(s3'-0.8) = 1.8142422, 1.8071455, 1.8003275 (65.20, ...).
5. Flint second surface.
   - log[n_f/((n_f-1)s4)] = 0.4343731 - 1.8142422 gives 0.041699505, 0.041497714, 0.041309429.
   - Subtract 1/R4 = 0.035624295 to get 1/((n_f-1)F), with log 7.7835613, 7.7688910, 7.7547407.
   - Back focal distance F = 282.9160 (red), 282.9297 (mean), 282.9160 (violet). Red and violet coincide, i.e. the system is achromatised for these two colours; the secondary spectrum is 0.0137.
6. Side computations (top right). 6.5911492 = log(0.041699505 - 0.041309429 = 0.000390076), and 8.8075879 = 6.5911492 - 7.7835613. These are the log of the red-violet difference and of its ratio to 1/((n_f-1)F); presumably used for adjusting r''.

B. EXACT MARGINAL RAY. The ray comes in parallel to the axis with incidence angle i1 = 18 deg 30' at the first surface, i.e. height h = r sin i1 ~ 10.84. At each spherical surface of radius R (centre C), with the ray meeting the axis at distance p from C and inclined at angle u to the axis:
- sin i = p sin u / R;
- sin i' = (n1/n2) sin i;
- u' = u + i - i' or u - (i' - i), according to the configuration;
- the new axis crossing is at p' = R sin i'/sin u' from C;
- convert to vertex distance, subtract thickness or gap, and re-reference to the next centre.

Step by step (first colour; the other columns are identical in form):
1. log sin i1 = 9.5014764. Subtract log n to get log sin i1' = 9.3241281, so i1' = 12 deg 10'35.639". Then u1 = i1 - i1' = 6 deg 19'24.361".
2. CP1 = r sin i1'/sin u1: 0.8575554 - 9.0419484 gives 65.40441. Vertex distance = 65.40441 + 34.15287 = 99.55728; Gauss computes this as 65.40441 - 2 = 63.40441, then + r = 97.55728 from the second vertex.
3. Distance to the centre of r': 101.33007 - 97.55728 = 3.77279 (log 0.5766626).
   - sin i2 = 3.77279 sin u1/r', log 7.6128727.
   - sin i2' = n sin i2, log 7.7902210.
   - i2 = 14'5.861", i2' = 21'12.474", difference 7'6.593".
   - u2 = 6 deg 26'30.954".
4. p2' = r' sin i2'/sin u2: 9.7959593 - 9.0499781 gives 5.57161. Then 101.33007 - 5.57161 = 95.75846 behind the crown; minus the gap gives 95.25846.
5. Flint first surface. p = 95.25846 - 42.06817 = 53.19029 (log 1.7258324).
   - log sin i3 = 9.1518568, log sin i3' = 9.1518568 - 0.1991543 = 8.9527025.
   - i3 = 8 deg 9'19.551", i3' = 5 deg 8'43.009", difference 3 deg 0'36.542".
   - u3 = 9 deg 27'7.496".
   - p' = R3 sin i3'/sin u3 = 22.97329. Vertex distance 42.06817 + 22.97329 = 65.04146; minus 0.8 gives 64.24146.
6. Flint second surface. p = 64.24146 - 28.07073 = 36.17073 (log 1.5583573).
   - log sin i4 = 9.3255367, log sin i4' = 9.3255367 + 0.1991543 = 9.5246910.
   - i4 = 12 deg 13'0.237", i4' = 19 deg 33'21.424", difference 7 deg 20'21.187".
   - u4 = u3 - 7 deg 20'21.187" = 2 deg 6'46.309".
   - p' = R4 sin i4'/sin u4: 0.9729447 - 8.5666504 gives 254.8557.
   - Marginal back focus = 254.8557 + 28.0707 = 282.9264.

RESULTS.
- Other colours (old radii): 254.8798 + 28.0707 = 282.9505 (mean, from the recomputed far-right column) and 254.8519 + 28.0707 = 282.9226 (violet).
- The top list gives paraxial vs marginal: 282.9160/282.9264, 282.9297/282.9505, 282.9160/282.9226. The longitudinal spherical aberration is +0.0104, +0.0208, +0.0066 (as written on the next page).
- Right-hand block, the same trace with R3 = 42.07205, R4 = 28.07232: marginal 282.9309, 282.9558, 282.9289. The next page gives the corresponding paraxial values 282.9269, 282.9404, 282.9269, so the aberrations become +0.0041, +0.0154, +0.0020.
- The next page then interpolates (factor 5/9) to final radii 42.07388/28.07307 and repeats the trace for a 13 deg ray, i.e. a zonal ray.
errors: Column 1, crown second surface: 21'12.474" - 14'5.861" = 7'6.613", but Gauss writes 7'6.593". The 0.02" slip propagates into u2 = 6 deg 26'30.954" (should be ~30.974"); it is negligible for the result.

Middle colour, first (old-radius) flint trace: the log of the fourth-surface distance was first taken as 1.5459636 (correct value ~1.5459600). The difference 19 deg 32'27.949" - 12 deg 3'10.717" is 7 deg 29'17.232", but 7 deg 29'16.232" was written (a 1" slip). The resulting 2 deg 6'39.681" and 254.89.. are wrong. Gauss himself recomputed this column on the far right (1.5459595, 7 deg 29'15.951", 2 deg 6'39.961", 254.8798 giving 282.9505) and struck out the earlier 282.9605.

Otherwise every addition and subtraction of angles and logarithms that I checked is consistent. The paraxial chain was checked independently: it reproduces 101.86977, 99.14918, 1/R3 = 0.0237709, 1/R4 = 0.0356243 and F = 282.916.

results.what: Paraxial back focal distance of a four-surface crown/flint meniscus doublet for three colours, computed in reduced-vergence form 1/((n-1)s); red and violet foci made to coincide (282.9160).
results.modern_name: Paraxial (Gaussian) ray trace / achromatisation of a doublet
results.usually_credited_to: Achromatic doublet: Hall/Dollond (1730s-1750s); paraxial surface-by-surface formulas: Euler, Klügel, Lagrange

results.what: Exact trigonometric ray trace of a marginal ray (incidence 18 deg 30' at the first surface) through all four surfaces with 7-place logarithms; comparison with the paraxial focus gives the longitudinal spherical aberration per colour (+0.0104, +0.0208, +0.0066).
results.modern_name: Trigonometric (finite) ray tracing; longitudinal spherical aberration
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euler/Klügel era); systematised later by Seidel, Steinheil and others

results.what: Fine adjustment of the flint radii (42.06817 to 42.07205, 28.07073 to 28.07232) to reduce the spherical aberration of a double-meniscus objective, followed by interpolation (next page).
results.modern_name: Gauss objective (two meniscus lenses, spherical aberration corrected for two colours)
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss, Zeitschrift für Astronomie 4 (1817)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the numerical working behind Gauss's own published 1817 double-meniscus objective: paraxial and trigonometric ray traces done by standard methods. It is a nice unpublished computational record showing the actual design values and residual aberrations, but nothing here is new relative to what is credited to him.
